posts.author: Incoherent
posts.content_md:
Howdy all

I thought I had posted yesterday, but my computer illiteracy seems to have kicked in and the video I wanted to show appears to be as of yet unposted.....

o I will try again - this time with a better description of my situation - I have obstinately been trying to make a decent hologram with my 15mw 532nm DPSS module (complete with noisy fan that keeps it mounted across the room) - across the room into a ~ 36x19 tupperwarelike sandbox. I recently had the opportunity to (using my beamsplitting piece of glass) mirror some beams straight back and turn my split beam arrangement into a michelsonish interferometer that showed me A. my setup is stable and B. settling time is no joke.

Images I had been getting on VRP-M plates had tended toward the blue and faint (even before adequete vibration measures) and after the introduction of the sandbox became notably less spectral though still dim and blue. Occasional and apparently accidental images in greenish showed up, though rife with issues and not quite holograms. I brought up the idea of a matte black dummy plate to a very helpful online buddy, and described my light at the plate as "an even green sheen" seemingly equal in intensity on both sides of the plate.

He said HMM, nifty idea, but it sounds like you have a 1:1 ratio at your plate, while a 10:1 is actually what you want for reflection holography, with the reference beam doing most of the work.

What the hell? Sounds funky, I thought it was an interference patern that would be clearest with equal light making it, but I'll give it a shot......

So I zoomed my Frankenstein reference beam lens in closer to my plate and stepped up the intensity. 

It was at this point that my plates in the developer turned a purty solid black, then bleached to a clear plate with a brown tint and a strange oil smoke haze,

...and dried into holograms!

For the first time I had an idea of what I might be looking at even before the plate was sprayed black on the back, and these were also the first that belyed an image even under inappropriate light! Very exciting 

I seem to be about where I want to be with a 15 second exposure, and plan to continue to play with relative beam intensities to discover what effects it has on color - I bring this up beacuse if you watch the video below, you will note a strong element of blueness that I hope to massage out of my setup. It has been brought to my attention that often the blue is a result of emulsion shrinkage, and I have begun to wonder if presoaking might be good for me....

Or do I just need to get exposures right?......still learning.....

Appreciate any insight 

Please watch my grainy video: [http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8xY_K-z6ATE](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8xY_K-z6ATE)

posts.author: dave battin
posts.content_md:
“I brought up the idea of a matte black dummy plate to a very helpful online buddy, and described my light at the plate as "an even green sheen" seemingly equal in intensity on both sides of the plate. “

What is the purpose of this?

”He said HMM, nifty idea, but it sounds like you have a 1:1 ratio at your plate, while a 10:1 is actually what you want for reflection holography, with the reference beam doing most of the work. “

You would like to have a 1:1 ratio, although it doesn’t always follow this rule…..

Like a bright shiny object, or strong master (H2) ,and it really depends on how you read the intensity at the plate. I always bracket shoot after all new set-ups (multiple exposure test shots).

”It was at this point that my plates in the developer turned a purity solid black, then bleached to a clear plate with a brown tint and a strange oil smoke haze, 

...and dried into holograms! “

When I was doing silver film I was told to try for a 3 minute developer time to go to black, this would mean my exposure was near correct, now some are as short 60 seconds. Again bracketing will speed thing up, (in the long run that is)!

”I seem to be about where I want to be with a 15 second exposure, and plan to continue to play with relative beam intensities to discover what effects it has on color .”

Based on the blue I see in your video you are in Very good shape < strong blue reflection hologram indicate exposure processing are good ,now all you have to do is or pre swell or a post swell your film , using TEA solutions (triethanolomine) read up in the WIKI areas

I believe some here on the forum have used sugar as a swelling agent, as a starting point ,try a pre soak using water and see what happens ………..

Good luck

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
> **Incoherent:** The matte black dummy plate...? A tool for Eyeballin' It. Not quite as effective as a white plate, but just another example of one of my attempts to compare beam ratios by eye.... Also nice for finding the brightest part of a diverging reference beam through a junky lens

How will a black plate help with this? It would reflect very little light. If you don't have a white "plate" just use a piece of paper or white or light cardboard.

> **Incoherent:** So cool. Swell that emulsion. Dig. Cool. Yep. When I look at light reflected from the emulsion on one of my holograms (mostly transmission lately), it is clear that the material has swelled

What about the transmission hologram is leading you to the conclusion that the emulsion has swelled? I'm not suggesting that it hasn't, just want to try to verify your conclusion.

> **Incoherent:** Cool but what happens when the emulsion unswells?

If you're making a transmission hologram it will reconstruct at a smaller angle. If you're making a reflection, it will reconstruct at a shorter wavelength.

posts.author: ErichRose
posts.content_md:
I don't get the logic of a black dummy plate. May I suggest:

Make yourself a white card with cross hairs that fits in the plate holder. Flat white matte board is good or even better "museum" board which has a solid white color and is excellent for building models as well as target cards. When setting up, start with the staright laser beam (no lense yet) centered on the card. Then insert the lense. All should then line up well. 

It isn't too hard to eye-ball intensity ratios on white card. To a great extent everything is relative. The higher ratio is important when you have extra shiny objects that might create hot-spots that would throw the ratio too far the other way. By example a pile of sparkly glass marbles might look better recorded with a 10:1 ratio versus all flat white objects set back from the plate which could be exposed closer to 1:1. Please someone jump in here if they have a better way of explaining this. It took me a number of plates before I understood that one.

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
> **ErichRose:** By example a pile of sparkly glass marbles might look better recorded with a 10:1 ratio versus all flat white objects set back from the plate which could be exposed closer to 1:1.

A better way to control strong specular hilights is to get a 1/2 wave plate and rotate the polarization to reduce the contribution from the reflections.
